lesson.title: Spans and subspaces

steps.headline: A span is every vector you can build from some vectors by scaling and adding. Its dimension counts the independent directions.

lead.text: c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ is a linear combination of v₁ and v₂. All such combinations together form their span. A span may be a line (dimension 1), a plane (dimension 2) or more.
Two vectors give two directions to move in, unless one of them is just a scaled copy of the other.

reveal.text: You checked whether the second vector adds a direction. A scaled copy gives nothing new, so the span stays a line.

workedSteps.text: Match the second coordinates. Only (1, 1) has an up part.
Match the first coordinates: c₁ + c₂ = 7.

steps.headline: Write (5, 3) as c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1). Find c₁.

workedSteps.text: Match the first coordinates: c₁ + 3 = 5. What is c₁?

lead.text: Compare the two vectors. Is one a multiple of the other, positive or negative?

reveal.text: You found the second vector is a negative multiple of the first. It points back along the same line, so the span is still one line.

steps.headline: A subspace contains the zero vector and stays inside itself when you add members or scale them.

lead.text: A subspace is a set of vectors with two properties. It contains the zero vector. Adding two members, or scaling one, gives another member. Every span is a subspace.
A drone must stay on the path y = 2x + 1. Any subspace has to contain the zero vector, so test the path with that.

lesson.orientation: Describe all linear combinations and test the conditions for a subspace.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A robot can only move in the direction (1, 2), any number of times, forwards or backwards.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the dimension of a span and test whether a set is a subspace.

recap.keyIdea: A span is every combination of some vectors, and its dimension counts the independent directions. A subspace contains zero and stays inside itself under adding and scaling.

blocks.text: You found that (1, 2) and (2, 4) span only a line, wrote (5, 3) with c₁ = 2, and ruled out y = 2x + 1 because it misses the origin.

recap.nextHook: Which vectors do you really need to span a space? Next: bases.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three moves of (1, 2) reach (3, 6), so y = 6.

questions.prompt: After some moves the robot is at x = 3. What is its y coordinate?
hints: Each move goes the same direction. What is the ratio of up to across?
For every one across the robot goes two up.
Scale up the whole move: three across means three moves.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds two to x. Each move goes two up for every one across, so scale both parts.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The robot stays on one line through the start, and every point on it is a multiple of (1, 2).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All multiples of one nonzero vector lie on one line, so the dimension is one.

questions.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of the single vector (3, 1)?
hints: What shape do all the multiples of one vector make?
Scaling a vector keeps it on one line.
Count the independent directions.

misconceptions.feedback: One vector gives one direction. Its multiples all lie on a single line.

questions.onCorrect: One nonzero vector gives a line: one independent direction.

questions.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of (1, 2) and (2, 4)?
hints: Is either vector a multiple of the other?
Compare the second vector with double the first.
If one is a scaled copy, it adds no new direction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second vector is twice the first, so their span is a line of dimension one.

misconceptions.feedback: The second vector is a multiple of the first, so it adds no new direction.

questions.onCorrect: The second vector is double the first, so the span stays a line.

acceptedIdeas: (1, 0) has second coordinate 0, so only c₂ contributes to it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (1, 0) has no up part, so the up part of the combination comes only from c₂(1, 1).

questions.prompt: Why can c₂ be found from the second coordinates alone?

choices.label: (1, 0) has second coordinate 0, so only c₂ contributes to it.
The second coordinates are always the largest.

hints: What is the second coordinate of (1, 0)?

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not matter. What matters is which vectors have an up part.
Here c₁ is not zero. It just has no say in the up coordinate.

questions.onCorrect: The first vector has no up part, so the up coordinate comes from c₂ alone.

questions.prompt: Write (5, 3) = c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1). What is c₁?
hints: Match the second coordinates first.
Then match the first coordinates.
The first coordinate of the combination is c₁ plus c₂.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second coordinate gives c₂ = 3; the first then gives c₁ = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is c₂. Put it into the first coordinates to find c₁.
That adds c₂ to the target. The target is c₁ plus c₂, so subtract.

questions.onCorrect: Match coordinates one at a time: c₂ from the second, then c₁ from the first.

questions.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of (2, 1) and (−4, −2)?
hints: Is either vector a multiple of the other?
Compare the second vector with the first.
A negative multiple still lies on the same line.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second vector is −2 times the first, so they span one line.

misconceptions.feedback: Check whether the second vector is a multiple of the first. It is.

questions.onCorrect: A negative multiple points back along the same line, so the span is one line.

questions.prompt: Is the set of points (x, y) with y = 2x a subspace of the plane?
hints: Is it a span of one vector? Does it contain zero?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. It is the span of (1, 2), so it contains zero and is closed.

misconceptions.feedback: That set is the span of (1, 2). Every span is a subspace.

questions.onCorrect: It is all multiples of (1, 2): a span, so a subspace.

questions.prompt: Is the set of points (x, y) with y = 2x + 1 a subspace of the plane?
hints: Does the set contain the zero vector?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The point (0, 0) gives y = 0, not 1, so zero is not in the set.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the zero vector. A subspace must contain it.

questions.onCorrect: Zero is not on the path, and every subspace must contain it.

questions.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of (1, 0) and (1, 1)?
hints: Is either vector a multiple of the other?
Compare their directions.
Two vectors in different directions span a plane.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: They are not scalar multiples, so they span a two-dimensional plane.

misconceptions.feedback: The second vector is not a multiple of the first, so it adds a new direction.

questions.onCorrect: Two vectors in different directions span the whole plane.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second coordinate gives c₂ = 4; the first then gives c₁ = 9 − 4 = 5.

questions.prompt: Write (9, 4) = c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1). What is c₁?
hints: Match the second coordinates first.
Then match the first coordinates.
The first coordinate of the combination is c₁ plus c₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is c₂. Put it into the first coordinates to find c₁.
That adds c₂ to the target. The target is c₁ plus c₂, so subtract.

questions.onCorrect: Match coordinates one at a time: c₂ from the second, then c₁ from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Neither is a multiple of the other, so the two vectors give two directions.

questions.prompt: What is the dimension of the span of (1, 2) and (3, 1)?
hints: Is either vector a multiple of the other?
Compare the ratio of up to across in each.
Two vectors in different directions span a plane.

misconceptions.feedback: Check whether either vector is a multiple of the other. Neither is.

questions.onCorrect: The vectors point in different directions, so they span a plane.
